sermons.life_context: Bishop Martin Benson had ordained him deacon at Gloucester a week earlier, on Trinity Sunday, 20 June 1736. He had not yet taken his Oxford BA, which followed in July 1736. By his own account he had been converted in the spring of 1735, after a long spiritual struggle and a breakdown in health.

Still a deacon, he had spent 1737 preaching in Gloucester, the west of England, Bristol and London. He was about to leave for Georgia, where from May 1738 he would serve as the Trustees' minister of Savannah.

Still a deacon, he had embarked for Georgia at the end of December 1737, according to Gillies. That same day, 7 May 1738, began his service as the Georgia Trustees' minister of Savannah, which lasted until 28 August 1738, when he left for England to raise funds and seek priest's orders.

Still a deacon, he served as the Georgia Trustees' minister of Savannah from 7 May to 28 August 1738, then returned to England to raise funds and seek priest's orders. He was ordained priest in January 1739, with the Savannah post as his title.

The sermon itself is undated. Gillies places his Kennington Common preaching in 1739, the year he was ordained priest in January, first preached in the open air to Kingswood coal miners near Bristol in February and, excluded from London pulpits, took his field preaching to Moorfields in April. He sailed for America again that August.

Back in England since March 1741, he had broken publicly with John Wesley over predestination and had been preaching from the new Moorfields Tabernacle in London, opened that April. This sermon belongs to his first visit to Scotland; two months later, on 14 November 1741, he married Elizabeth James, a widow of Abergavenny, at Caerphilly in Wales.

He was on his third American visit, having sailed from Plymouth with his wife Elizabeth in August 1744, six months after their only child, John, was buried at Gloucester, and reached New York that October. He stayed in the colonies, itinerating through them, until June 1748.

A domestic chaplain to the Countess of Huntingdon since the late 1740s, he preached chiefly from the Moorfields Tabernacle and his Tottenham Court Road chapel. His wife Elizabeth had died in August 1768, a year before this farewell, and was buried in that chapel. He was about to embark on his seventh and final voyage to America.

He was on his seventh and final American visit, having embarked shortly after his last English sermons at Ramsgate in September 1769, and had preached at Charleston and Savannah. He had begun building the Bethesda orphan house near Savannah in March 1740, nearly thirty years earlier. His wife Elizabeth had died in August 1768.
